newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey right says alliance strong despite attacks.
newsitem.headline: Turkey right says alliance strong despite attacks.

text.p: Turkey's conservative party said on Thursday its coalition with the Islamists was solid despite speculation of a rift over religious issues and attacks from leftist MPs and the armed forces.

"As long as our partner complies with the coalition protocol, I do not see that there will be any problems in the government...And given that there are no problems with the protocol, the government will continue with its duties," said Hayri Kozakcioglu, deputy chairman of the True Path Party (DYP).
He was quoted on the state-run Anatolian news agency following a meeting of the DYP executive.

Two leftist parties have filed censure motions against the government to "safeguard the secular system" and the army put on a show of force this week by parading tanks through an Islamist-held district where an anti-Israeli protest had taken place.

The Islamist Welfare Party of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has alarmed the secularist elite with proposals during the Moslem holy month of Ramadan to lift a ban on Islamic headscarves for women civil servants and pave the road for overland pilgrimages to the Moslem holy city of Mecca.
Other measures include construction of mosques in historic secularist strongholds, including the Christian quarter of the former Ottoman capital.
Kozakcioglu said there would be no change in the headscarf rule and that Welfare had submitted no proposal to the cabinet on that or other disputed issues.
The anti-Israeli protest in Ankara's Sincan district added to the unease with Welfare. Police on Wednesday arrested the mayor of Sincan, Bekir Yildiz, for hosting the event.

President Suleyman Demirel said in an interview with TGRT television that the Sincan incident was "unfortunate", but he gave reassurance that speculation of a military coup to remove the Islamists from office was inappropriate.

"Finally there is a government here, and this government depends on the confidence vote of the parliament. The rules are working," he said. "It is up to parliament whether it likes (the government) of not."
He said if the situation demanded it, it would be more appropriate for the president to dissolve parliament and call early elections than for the generals to take over.
Turkey's military staged three coups between 1960 and 1980.
Demirel, who was dislodged as premier in two of the coups, said they had solved nothing.

"Turkey has not been able to heal its wounds from the past. It cannot suffer new wounds," he said. "It is very wrong for politicians and the media to discuss a coup...Let us keep politics out of the school, the barracks and the mosque."
